title: Episode 42: Deadwood and the Dead Man's Hand: Wild Bill Hickok
description:
In 1876, the illegal gold rush into the sacred Black Hills of Lakota Sioux territory created Deadwood, South Dakota: a lawless gulch of saloons, brothels, and gunslingers. In August 1876, legendary scout and gunfighter James Butler 'Wild Bill' Hickok sat down for a game of poker in Nuttal & Mann's Saloon No. 10, holding a pair of aces and a pair of eights when Jack McCall shot him in the back of the head.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the summer of eighteen seventy-six, while the United States was celebrating the centennial of the Declaration of Independence in Philadelphia, a violent, illegal drama was unfolding in the Black Hills of southwestern South Dakota. Guaranteed to the Lakota Sioux in perpetuity by the Treaty of eighteen sixty-eight, the sacred Paha Sapa was invaded by thousands of gold-crazed prospectors following George Armstrong Custer's expedition. In a narrow, pine-choked gulch filled with dead timber, an explosive, lawless boomtown erupted: Deadwood. It was a frontier Babylon where gold dust was the currency, murder was a weekly occurrence, and law and order did not exist. Into this dangerous cauldron rode the premier scout, marksman, and gunfighter of the American West: James Butler 'Wild Bill' Hickok. On an August afternoon in a smoke-filled saloon, a game of poker and a cowardly shot from behind created the most famous card hand in Western history. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: GOLD IN THE SACRED BLACK HILLS
In eighteen seventy-four, Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer led a military reconnaissance expedition of over one thousand cavalry, artillerymen, and scientific experts deep into the uncharted Black Hills of southwestern Dakota Territory. Known to the Lakota Sioux as Paha Sapa—the sacred heart of everything that is—the Black Hills were a pine-covered island of granite peaks rising majestically from the rolling sea of grass, guaranteed to the Native tribes in perpetuity under the solemn Fort Laramie Treaty of eighteen sixty-eight. But when Custer's expedition prospectors discovered rich placer gold along French Creek, Custer fired off sensational dispatches to newspapers, declaring that gold was present 'from the grass roots down.' Despite federal treaties, an unstoppable stampede of tens of thousands of gold-crazed prospectors, saloon keepers, gamblers, and outlaws poured into the forbidden hills, provoking furious, bloody resistance from Lakota warriors led by Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse. By the spring of eighteen seventy-six, the center of the gold rush shifted to the northern hills, where prospectors struck fabulously rich gravel in a deep, narrow canyon choked with burned dead timber. The settlement took the name of Deadwood. Within months, more than ten thousand miners, madams, and gunslingers packed into the muddy gulch, creating a roaring, lawless boomtown governed strictly by the six-shooter. Thousands of prospectors poured illegally into the sacred Black Hills following Custer eighteen seventy-four expedition, staking claims in the narrow limestone gulch that became Deadwood.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE LIVING LEGEND: WILD BILL HICKOK
In July eighteen seventy-six, just weeks after Custer and his Seventh Cavalry were wiped out at the Battle of the Little Bighorn, a colorful wagon train rolled down Deadwood's muddy main street, led by the premier scout and gunfighter of the American frontier: thirty-nine-year-old James Butler Hickok, known to the world as 'Wild Bill.' Standing six feet tall, with broad shoulders, narrow waist, flowing auburn hair that fell over his shoulders in frontier fashion, and cold blue eyes, Hickok was an invincible living legend. During the Civil War, he had served as a Union cavalry scout and sharpshooter; in eighteen sixty-five in Springfield, Missouri, he had killed Dave Tutt in the first documented quick-draw duel in Western history; and as the fearless marshal of Hays City and Abilene, Kansas, he had tamed violent Texas cowboys with his twin silver-plated, ivory-handled Colt forty-four revolvers worn backwards in a silk sash. Accompanying Hickok into Deadwood was another legendary character: Martha Jane Canary, universally known as 'Calamity Jane'—a foul-mouthed, tobacco-chewing twenty-four-year-old scout clad in fringed buckskin who worshipped Wild Bill with unrequited devotion. Hickok had come to Deadwood hoping to secure a modest gold claim to support his new bride, circus owner Agnes Lake Thatcher, but his true home remained the smoky saloon and the green-felt poker table. Hickok was famous from dime novels and frontier scouts across Kansas, renowned for his lightning-quick draw with twin ivory-handled Colt eighteen fifty-one Navy revolvers worn butts-forward in a red silk sash.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SHADOW OF FAILING SIGHT
Beneath his glamorous, invincible reputation, Wild Bill was a weary, aging warrior living in the shadow of tragedy. Years of saloon smoke, gunsmoke, and heavy drinking had taken a severe toll on his health. More critically, Hickok was suffering from incipient glaucoma, which was gradually dimming his legendary vision. In Deadwood, Hickok spent his afternoons and evenings playing poker in the town's numerous drinking establishments, most notably Nuttal and Mann's Saloon Number Ten. Hickok was acutely aware that dozens of young, reckless gunslingers and outlaws frequented Deadwood, eager to make an instant frontier reputation by killing the famous Wild Bill. To protect himself against ambush, Hickok adhered to an unbreakable personal rule: whenever he sat down at a card table, he always chose a chair that positioned his back firmly against a solid wall, allowing him to watch every person who entered the saloon door with his hands resting near his revolvers. Hickok always insisted on sitting with his back to the wall so he could watch the saloon entrance, but on August second, the only available chair at the card table placed his back toward the open doorway.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE FATAL HAND IN SALOON NO. 10
On the warm afternoon of Wednesday, August second, eighteen seventy-six, Hickok walked into Saloon Number Ten for an afternoon game of five-card draw poker with riverboat captain William Massie, miner Charlie Rich, and saloon owner Carl Mann. When Hickok approached the table, he noticed that the only vacant seat was facing the front door, leaving his back exposed to the rear of the saloon. Hickok asked Charlie Rich twice to change seats with him, but Rich laughed and refused to move. Reluctantly, violating his own lifelong rule for the first time in his life, Hickok took the exposed chair. Around four o'clock in the afternoon, a drunken, cross-eyed young drifter named Jack McCall entered the saloon. McCall, nicknamed 'Broken Nose Jack,' had lost heavily in a poker game with Hickok the previous evening, and Hickok had generously given the humiliated youth a dollar to buy breakfast, warning him not to play again until he had money. Nursing a sullen, drunken grudge, McCall slipped quietly along the bar behind Hickok's back. Pulling a forty-five caliber Colt single-action revolver from his pocket, McCall leveled the barrel just inches from the back of Hickok's head and screamed: 'Damn you, take that!' McCall pulled the trigger; the bullet passed clean through Hickok's brain and lodged in Captain Massie's wrist. Jack McCall slipped unnoticed through the batwing doors, pulled a forty-five caliber revolver from his coat, and shouted 'Take that!' before firing directly into the back of Hickok head at point-blank range.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE DEAD MAN'S HAND
Wild Bill Hickok died instantly, his head slumping forward onto the green felt table without uttering a sound. As his body slipped from the chair onto the wooden sawdust floor, his fingers relaxed, dropping the cards he had been holding face up onto the table. They were two black aces—the ace of spades and the ace of clubs—and two black eights—the eight of spades and the eight of clubs—with an unrevealed fifth card, remembered by witnesses as either the queen of clubs or the nine of diamonds. That exact combination—a pair of aces and a pair of eights, all black—became immortalized in gaming lore across the world as the 'Dead Man's Hand.' McCall ran out into the street, waving his smoking pistol and attempting to escape on a horse, but the saddle cinch broke, and he was quickly captured hiding in the back of a butcher shop by enraged miners. The cards slipped from Hickok lifeless fingers onto the sawdust floor: the black aces and black eights that became forever immortalized across the world as the Dead Man Hand.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE MINERS' COURT AND THE TRUE HANGING
Because Deadwood was situated on unceded Lakota Sioux territory, civil United States courts had no jurisdiction in the illegal camp. The miners immediately convened an impromptu miners' court in the theater, appointing a judge, prosecutor, and defense counsel. McCall took the stand and concocted a bizarre, fabricated defense, claiming that Wild Bill had killed his brother in Kansas years earlier, and that he had acted in family revenge. The miners' jury, sympathetic to the revenge defense and anxious to return to their gold sluices, astonishingly acquitted McCall of murder! McCall quickly fled the Black Hills, bragging openly in Wyoming saloons that he had killed the great Wild Bill. But his boast proved his undoing. Federal authorities arrested McCall in Laramie, ruling that an illegal miners' court on an Indian reservation held no double jeopardy protection under federal law. McCall was retried for murder in the United States District Court in Yankton, convicted of first-degree murder, and hanged on March first, eighteen seventy-seven, becoming the first person legally executed in Dakota Territory. McCall was later arrested by federal marshals in Wyoming, retried under federal jurisdiction, and hanged in Yankton for the cowardly murder.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: MOUNT MORIAH AND THE LEGEND OF WILD BILL
Wild Bill Hickok was buried by his friends in the Ingelside Cemetery, and later reinterred in the picturesque Mount Moriah Cemetery perched high on the pine-covered bluffs overlooking Deadwood. In nineteen oh-three, when Calamity Jane died in a Deadwood boarding house, her final dying request was granted: she was buried directly beside Wild Bill, where the two frontier legends rest together for eternity. Today, Deadwood is a thriving National Historic Landmark, where the historic cobblestone streets, Victorian brick facades, and Saloon Number Ten still recreate the dramatic days of eighteen seventy-six. Wild Bill Hickok's death marked the end of the romantic era of the frontier gunfighter—a man who lived by the gun, tamed the wildest camps of the West, and entered eternity with a pair of aces and eights in his hand.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Wild Bill Hickok and the legend of Deadwood capture the romantic, dangerous essence of the American frontier. It shows how myth and reality intertwined in the mining camps, leaving behind legends that outlived the gold that drew them there. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we witness the monumental sculpting of Mount Rushmore. Until then, stay curious.
